title: Falling and Catching in a Trot: A Body on Two Feet as an Inverted Pendulum, and How Long a Stance May Last Before the Next Feet Must Land

questions.question: Why is a trot always falling?
options: With two feet down there is no support polygon, only a line, and the body falls toward one side until the other pair lands
The body's speed carries it past the feet at every step
The legs are too short to hold the body level
The diagonal feet slip sideways under the load
questions.explanation: Two feet make a line, not an area. The centre of mass is never exactly over a line, so the body is always turning about it, and the gait works by landing the other pair in time.

questions.question: A body 10 mm off the line took how long to fall 6 cm?
options: 0.166 s, one time constant
questions.explanation: It starts slowly because the push away from the line is proportional to the distance from it. From 30 mm it took 0.22 s, and 0.15 s if it was already moving away.

questions.question: What does a taller body do?
options: Falls faster, because it has further to go
Falls in the same time: the time depends only on the offset
Falls more slowly: 0.50 s for 0.40 m
Falls more slowly, in proportion to its height
questions.explanation: The time constant is the square root of the height over g, so a taller body is slower, but only by the square root: 0.50 s at 0.40 m against 0.41 s at 0.27 m.

questions.question: A stance of 0.25 s with the centre 30 mm off the line was:
options: Short enough, with a margin of 0.7
Too long (it falls first)
Short enough, but with no margin
Too long for either offset
questions.explanation: From 30 mm the body is 6 cm out after 0.22 s, before a 0.25 s stance ends. From 10 mm the same stance was short enough.

questions.question: What does a negative time mean?
options: The body has already fallen past the limit
The quadratic has no real root, so there is no answer
The offset was measured from the wrong side of the line
The centre is moving back toward the line fast enough that it never gets there
questions.explanation: A body moving back toward the line can stop and turn before it gets out to the limit. The closed form marks that case with a negative time.

questions.question: What is not in the model?
options: The height of the body
The speed the centre already has
The distance at which the swing feet must be down
Where the swing feet land and the body's rotation
questions.explanation: The model is one point mass falling sideways about a line. It says how long there is, not where the next pair of feet should go; that is 35-07.
